title: How to Make LinkedIn Work Harder So You Don't Have To!
description:
What if you could make LinkedIn work harder so YOU don't have to? If you're tired of applying for jobs, messaging recruiters, and hearing nothing back, it might be time to rethink your LinkedIn job search strategy.

In this video, I'm sharing 3 simple LinkedIn strategies to help you get noticed by recruiters, increase your visibility, and attract more job opportunities without spending hours on LinkedIn every day.

You'll learn how to:
 Optimize your LinkedIn profile with keywords recruiters actually search for.
 Showcase your accomplishments so employers see your value.
 Build visibility and professional connections without cold messaging everyone.

Stop chasing every opportunity. Start making LinkedIn work for you.

If your resume is what’s keeping you stuck, check out my Get Seen System. It walks you through creating a stronger, more strategic resume that gets noticed!

transcript: Most job seekers are stuck in this cycle. Find a job, apply, find another job, apply, send a recruiter a message, get ghosted, send another message, never hear again, apply again, and every opportunity feels like you are starting from zero. But, what if the answer on LinkedIn is not doing more? What if it's doing less, but making the things you do keep working for you? Because the goal should not be spending 3 hours every night trying to get in front of recruiters, the goal is to build your LinkedIn so recruiters, hiring managers, and people in your industry start finding you. And if you are doing all the LinkedIn things and still hearing crickets, there's a good chance you are doing too much of the wrong work. Let's get in and fix it. My name is Kate Currier, career strategist to 100 years in, and here's what we're going to start with. Stop polishing your LinkedIn and start making it searchable. Think of LinkedIn a little bit like Google for recruiters. Recruiters are searching for job titles, specialized skills, tools, industry experience, certifications, and technology. So, you can have a beautifully written profile, but if you're not using the language they are actually searching for, you may never be making it into the results. So, ask yourself this simple question. What would someone type into LinkedIn if they were trying to find somebody like me? If you're targeting social media marketing, marketing is way too broad. Think social media manager, B2B, SaaS, SEO, paid social, meta ads, HubSpot, content strategies, lead generations. Those are the kinds of terms that tell LinkedIn and the person searching exactly where you fit. And I want those words showing up in your headline. So, instead of just marketing professional, creative thinker, results-driven leader, try something more like social media marketing manager, B2B, SaaS, SEO plus paid social, grew organic traffic 62% and reduced acquisition costs by 80%. Now, I know what you do, what you specialize in, and you already gave me a reason to keep reading cuz I see the value you added. One of the easiest ways to find the right keywords is to pull up five to 10 job descriptions for jobs you would actually want and look for repetition. What titles keep appearing? What tools are they mentioning? What skills do they want to use? What terminology is used? If seven out of 10 jobs mention the same thing and you genuinely have that skill, it probably belongs right on your LinkedIn profile. And here's another trick I love, reverse search people who were recently hired into the exact role you're looking for. Look at a handful of their profiles. What language are they using? What skills keep showing up? What tools are they mentioning? What accomplishments? You will start seeing patterns fast. I have another video where I walk through that reverse search process step-by-step, so I will go ahead and link that. It's right above. Make sure to watch that one next. So, now that you know the language your market is using, work it naturally into your headline, your about section, your experience and skills. And hey, if this kind of practical job search advice is helpful, make sure to hit that like and subscribe. Now, the second shift is this, stop telling employers what you did and show them what happened because you did it. And this is what I mean when I say bring the receipts. Most LinkedIn profiles read like job description, manage projects, work with customers, created social media campaigns. Okay, but what happened? Instead of manage social media campaigns across multiple platforms, give me built and managed a multi-platform content strategy that increased organic engagement 48% in 6 months. Instead of responsible for onboarding new employees, give me redesigned the onboarding process cutting average ramp up from 6 weeks to four. Your receipts do not have to be giant revenue numbers. Just think about processes you've improved, problems you've solved, the time you saved, the goals you exceeded, the client outcome you improved, the project you rescued, or the thing that your coworkers and managers always come to you for. That is the stuff employers actually remember. And collect your recommendations, too, because now someone beside you is saying, "Yep, this person really does what they say they do, and they're pretty darn good at it." I also have a video on how to move recommendations higher on your profile, even without premium, so I will link that, too. At this point, we have made you easier to find, more compelling when somebody clicks, and now comes the part where the whole do less idea really starts paying off. You do not have to wait for people to search for you. You can start showing up in their feed. And no, I'm not telling you to become a LinkedIn influencer, I'm telling you to become visible in your industry. Start with 5 to 10 companies you would genuinely love to work for. Follow them. Then find maybe 10 to 15 people in your field who post regularly and actually have something interesting to say. Now, instead of randomly scrolling LinkedIn for an hour, you have a small curated group of people and companies worth paying attention to. But when you're making a comment, please don't simply write great post with a fun little confetti blower. You want to show up like an industry peer, not their hype squad. So, let's say a company announces they're expanding into healthcare. Instead of "Hey, congratulations, so exciting," you could say, "Really interesting to see the expansion into healthcare. When our team moved into a new vertical, one of the biggest surprises was how much our messaging had to change, even though the product stayed the same. Are you finding that with this launch, too?" That comment quietly does a lot. You demonstrate experience, you added something useful, and you gave them an easy reason to respond. This is also why I like thoughtful comments before cold DMs, because if someone is actively posting, they want conversation. Your comment helps their post get more reach, so they are more motivated to comment back. Plus, other people can see it, and suddenly your networking is happening in public. So, have a couple of real exchanges in the comment section, and now send a message. It feels very different this way. You are no longer random stranger who wants something from me. You are Oh, yeah, I've seen this person before. They've made some great comments. And sometimes, you will not even have to make that first move. I've actually had people much, much bigger than me in my own industry follow me, or even reach out after I consistently engage with what they were posting. And I remember thinking, why does this person even know who I am? But, that is the point. Visibility compounds. And now, once commenting starts feeling normal, start posting, too. And please stop putting pressure on yourself to sound brilliant. You don't need to go viral. You just need to give people a sense of what you know, what you care about, and the way you think, and why you would be of great value to them. Talk about a project you are working on, something you learned, a mistake you see people make in your industry, a professional accomplishment you're excited about, a change you see happening in your field, a tool you just learned to use, a lesson from a difficult project, and yes, occasionally be the human being. Post the dog, post the cat, tell everyone you destroyed your old college roommate at pickleball. People do not need a corporate robot. They need enough professional substance to understand your value, and enough personality to remember you. And this is where all this comes back to doing less. Remember the cycle we started with? Find job, apply, find another job, apply. Send recruiter message, get ignored, start over. That is a lot of work that is only working once. What we are doing instead is building an asset, a searchable profile, proof of what you could do, relationships in your industry, content that keeps working after you post it, and visibility that grows over time. So, instead of constantly asking, "How do I get in front of them?" you start creating more opportunities for people to think, "Who is this person?" And that is the real goal. Stop doing so much work that only works once. Make the work you do on LinkedIn keep working for you. So, remember these three simple shifts. Make your profile searchable, bring the receipts, and start showing up where the people and companies you care about already are. And if your resume needs the same kind of help making your value obvious quickly instead of just listing everything you've ever done, check out my Get Seen system. I'll link it below. And remember, the best LinkedIn strategy is not the one that gives you another 3 hours of work every night. It's the one where the work you do today keeps making you easier to find tomorrow. And if you want to learn the reverse search trick I mentioned earlier, the one that lets you see who companies are actually hiring and what those people have on their profiles, watch this video next. That's where I would start. Make sure to like and subscribe for practical job search strategy.
